title: Why AI Writing Still Reads Like Slop — Louis-François Bouchard, Towards AI
talk_summary: The speaker built a creative-writing benchmark (Tone-Bench) to measure 'slop' and shares practical findings on how to get better writing from models. Key transferable mechanisms: generate many cheap drafts and have a strong judge merge the best parts, use a single high-thinking reviewer pass (not loops), and beware LLM-judge self-preference when evaluating.

takeaways.technique: Many cheap drafts + strong judge merge
takeaways.what_they_do: Generate ~10 drafts with a cheap model, then have a smarter high-thinking judge merge the best parts of each draft instead of one expensive generation.
takeaways.evidence_quote: generate several drafts, like 10 drafts of one specific thing with a cheaper model... and then have a smarter high-thinking judge... merge the best parts of each of this these drafts
takeaways.numbers: GLM 5.3 flash cited as ~50x cheaper than best model; claims still cheaper than one Opus 5.5 generation

takeaways.technique: Single high-thinking reviewer pass, not loops
takeaways.what_they_do: Use one high-thinking judge model 1-3 times to give feedback to the writer; more iterations cause it to loop into slop.
takeaways.evidence_quote: use a high-thinking judge just one time, one to three times, otherwise it will loop into slap

takeaways.what_they_do: Found LLM judges prefer their own model family (OpenAI especially); recommends using a different model family as judge than the one being evaluated, plus human A/B spot-checks.
takeaways.evidence_quote: OpenAI really has a strong preference on its own family of models, not just one model, but all OpenAI models
takeaways.numbers: 1,000 human A/B pairs compared to calibrate judges

takeaways.what_they_do: Generate 5 drafts per task to measure variance; worse models have wider variance and occasional outlier-good generations.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we generate five of them... to check for intra-model variability... the worse the model is, the widest the variance
takeaways.numbers: 5 drafts per task as cost/variance middle ground

takeaways.technique: Long detailed prompt with positive and negative examples
takeaways.what_they_do: Feed extremely long prompts with many positive examples, negative examples, and explicit banned words/tone guidance; 'it cannot be long enough'.
takeaways.evidence_quote: have an extremely long and detailed prompt. It cannot be long enough, and the more the better... negative examples of things you don't like

takeaways.what_they_do: Judge first assigns a category (6 options) then a rating within it, with per-score examples; found this beats binary or direct percentage scoring for qualitative tasks.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the judge will categorize between six categories first and after having found a category, it will give a rating
